# Fundamentals and State of the Art {#sec-fundamentals}

This chapter explains the background that is needed to follow the rest of the thesis. It starts with the application, the lighting of an aircraft cabin (@sec-cabin-lighting). It then explains how LEDs work and how their brightness is controlled (@sec-led-dimming), how an FPGA is built (@sec-fpga-fundamentals) and how a design is brought onto an FPGA (@sec-design-flow). The last technical parts describe serial communication (@sec-serial-communication) and the Flexlink protocol (@sec-flexlink). The chapter ends with an overview of how the segments are controlled today and what the node of this thesis does differently (@sec-state-of-the-art).

## Aircraft Cabin Lighting {#sec-cabin-lighting}

Previously, the lighting system used for aircraft cabins came from fluorescent technology, and LEDs were first added only for *coloured mood lighting*. As the efficiency of LEDs increased, they became able to produce the white light as well [@krellera2009]. Currently, aircrafts such as the Airbus A380 and the Boeing 787 use LED cabin lighting systems that combine white light and coloured ones. LEDs are efficient with energy savings of 35 % to 55 % when compared to previous lighting systems, and a lifetime of about 50,000 hours, which is roughly ten times longer than that of incandescent, fluorescent or halogen lamps. Because LEDs are solid-state devices, they are also smaller, lighter and more resistant to vibration and shock, which reduces fuel consumption and maintenance. The colour control of LEDs allows the cabin light changes with the phase of the flight which is known as *light scenes*. For instance, bright light that imitates a sunrise in the morning, a bright, fresh light in the afternoon and a cool light in the evening. On long flights, such programmes are used to shift the sleep rhythm of the passengers slowly towards the time zone of the destination [@lumileds2015].

Electronic equipment for aircraft must meet strict rules. In the European Union, the **European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA)** is responsible for the certification of aircraft and their equipment. For the technical details, EASA and the U.S authorities rely on industry standards that are published jointly by EUROCAE in Europe and RTCA in the USA. EUROCAE ED-14G defines standard environmental test conditions and test procedures for airborne equipment [@eurocae_ed14g]. EUROCAE ED-80, which corresponds to RTCA DO-254, gives design assurance guidance for airborne electronic hardware, including complex programmable devices such as FPGAs. EASA recognises this standard in its Acceptable Means of Compliance *AMC 20-152A* [@easa_amc20152a]. Certification according to these documents is outside the scope of this thesis (@sec-scope), but they explain why reliability, simple and traceable design, and documented verification are important for any design that is meant for an aircraft.

## LEDs and LED Dimming {#sec-led-dimming}

### LED Basics {#sec-led-basics}

An LED is a semiconductor diode that emits light when a current flows through it in the forward direction. The voltage across the LED in this state is called the forward voltage $V_F$. It depends on the semiconductor material and therefore on the colour. In general, standard red, green and yellow LEDs have forward voltages of 1.4 V to 2.6 V, while blue, green (InGaN) and white LEDs need about 3.1 V to 4.0 V, depending on the manufacturer [@maxim2004]. @fig-led-iv shows the typical shape of the current-voltage curve. Below the forward voltage, almost no current flows. Above it, the current rises very steeply, so a small change of the voltage gives a large change of the current. For this reason, an LED is always operated with a resistor or a current source that limits the current [@schubert2006].

![Current-voltage curves of a red and a green/blue LED, drawn with a simple diode model. The points mark the typical forward voltages at 20 mA [@avago_hlmp_hx64].](images/ch2_led_iv_curve){#fig-led-iv width=80%}

### RGBW Colour Mixing {#sec-rgbw}

An LED emits light in a narrow range of wavelengths, so each LED has one fixed colour. In a typical 5 mm LED family, for example, the red LED has a dominant wavelength of 626 nm, the green LED 525 nm and the blue LED 470 nm [@avago_hlmp_hx64]. Other colours are made by mixing the light of several LEDs, and the colours that are mixed are called *primaries* [@doe_ledcolor2012]. When a red, a green and a blue LED (RGB) light up the same area, the eye sees one mixed colour, which depends on how bright each LED is compared with the other two (@fig-colour-mixing).

![Mixing the light of red, green and blue LEDs.](images/ch2_colour_mixing){#fig-colour-mixing width=60%}

White light can be produced by mixing red, green and blue, but they have a lower efficacy and less colour consistency because the red, green and blue LEDs lose brightness at different rates as they age. In general lighting, white LEDs are mostly made by phosphor conversion, a blue or near-ultraviolet LED chip is combined with a phosphor that emits yellow light. This combination of blue and yellow light blends together in the human eye to create white light [@doe_ledcolor2012]. Therefore, a fourth white LED is often added to the three coloured ones. The white LED provides the white light directly, while the coloured LEDs are used to set the colour.

The colour of white light is described by its **correlated colour temperature (CCT)**, given in kelvin (K). It is the temperature at which a heated *black body* would glow in the colour closest to that of the light source. A low CCT looks warm and yellowish, a high CCT cool and bluish [@doe_ledcolor2012]. With RGBW LEDs, both the colour and the colour temperature of the light are changed only by changing the brightness of the four channels. For the control electronics, RGBW therefore means four channels per segment, one for each colour, and the brightness of each channel must be set on its own. With a resolution of 16 bits, each channel has $2^{16} = 65{,}536$ brightness steps, from 0 (off) to 65,535 (full brightness). Setting each channel on its own is necessary because the same current does not give the same light output for every colour. At a current of 20 mA, the datasheet of the LED family mentioned above gives a luminous intensity of 1150 mcd to 2400 mcd for the red LED, 1990 mcd to 5040 mcd for the green LED and only 460 mcd to 1150 mcd for the blue LED [@avago_hlmp_hx64]. In addition, the light output and the colour of an LED change with its temperature and over its lifetime [@doe_ledcolor2012]. A system that keeps the mixed colour exact would therefore have to measure the temperature of each segment and correct the brightness values. This correction is not part of this thesis.

### PWM and Flickering {#sec-pwm-parameters}

A PWM signal is a square wave with a fixed period $T$. In each period, the signal is high for the time $t_\text{on}$ and low for the rest of the period. The *duty cycle* $D$ is the part of the period in which the signal is high:

$$
D = \frac{t_\text{on}}{T}
$$ {#eq-duty-cycle}

If the LED current during the on-time is $I_\text{LED}$, the average current, and with it the perceived brightness, changes in proportion to the duty cycle [@parasseril2006]:

$$
I_\text{avg} = D \cdot I_\text{LED}
$$ {#eq-avg-current}

For example, with $I_\text{LED} = 20\ \text{mA}$ and $D = 25\ \%$, the average current is
$I_\text{avg} = 0.25 \cdot 20\ \text{mA} = 5\ \text{mA}$.

@fig-pwm-duty shows two PWM signals with duty cycles of 25 % and 75 %.

![Ideal PWM signals with 25 % and 75 % duty cycle at $f_\text{PWM} \approx 763$ Hz.](images/ch2_pwm_duty_cycle){#fig-pwm-duty width=90%}

In a digital circuit, a PWM signal is usually made with a *counter* and a *comparator*. The counter counts clock cycles from $0$ to $2^N - 1$ and then starts again, where $N$ is the resolution in bits. The output is high while the counter value is smaller than the brightness value. With this simple rule, the largest value $2^N - 1$ would still leave the output low for one clock cycle in every period. The design in this thesis therefore treats the largest value as "always on" (@sec-rtl). One full count is one PWM period, so the PWM frequency is:

$$
f_\text{PWM} = \frac{f_\text{clk}}{2^N}
$$ {#eq-pwm-frequency}

With the values used in this thesis, $f_\text{clk} = 50\ \text{MHz}$ and $N = 16$:

1. Number of steps: $2^{16} = 65{,}536$.
2. PWM frequency: $f_\text{PWM} = 50{,}000{,}000\ \text{Hz} / 65{,}536 \approx 762.9\ \text{Hz}$.
3. PWM period: $T = 65{,}536 / 50{,}000{,}000\ \text{Hz} \approx 1.31\ \text{ms}$.
4. Smallest step, one clock cycle: $1 / 50\ \text{MHz} = 20\ \text{ns}$.

@eq-pwm-frequency shows the basic trade-off of digital PWM, for a fixed clock, every additional bit of resolution halves the PWM frequency.

Because the light of a PWM-dimmed LED is switched on and off, the light output changes over time. If this change is slow enough, people can see it as *flicker*, or it can lead to other effects such as stroboscopic effects [@ieee1789]. A common measure is the *percent flicker*:

$$
\text{Percent flicker} = 100\ \% \cdot \frac{L_\text{max} - L_\text{min}}{L_\text{max} + L_\text{min}}
$$ {#eq-percent-flicker}

where $L_\text{max}$ and $L_\text{min}$ are the highest and the lowest light output within one period. For a PWM signal that switches the LED fully off, $L_\text{min} = 0$, so the percent flicker is $100\ \%$ for every duty cycle below $100\ \%$.

The recommended practice IEEE 1789-2015 gives limits for flicker in LED lighting. Miller and Lehman explain how to apply it in a presentation for the Solid-State Lighting program of the U.S. Department of Energy. Lehman was the chair of the IEEE working group that wrote the recommended practice. For a flicker frequency of at least 100 Hz, the highest allowed percent flicker is the frequency multiplied by $0.08$. A product that stays below this value is acceptable for all but the most unusually sensitive persons, and at 1250 Hz or higher, 100 % flicker is allowed [@miller_lehman2015].

For the PWM frequency of this thesis:

1. Low-risk limit at 762.9 Hz: $0.08 \cdot 762.9 \approx 61\ \%$.
2. Percent flicker of full on-off PWM: $100\ \%$.
3. Since $100\ \% > 61\ \%$, a full on-off PWM at 762.9 Hz is above the low-risk level of IEEE 1789, although it meets the AES requirement of more than 400 Hz (Bronze) and more than 600 Hz (Silver).

This point is discussed again in the evaluation (@sec-evaluation).

### Low-Side Switching with a Transistor {#sec-low-side-switching}

An FPGA output cannot drive a typical LED directly. Its current is limited, and its voltage is lower than the forward voltage of the LED. For example, the blue and green LEDs mentioned above have a typical forward voltage of 3.2 V at 20 mA [@avago_hlmp_hx64], which is higher than the output level of about 2.5 V of the evaluation board used in this thesis (@sec-gatemate). In a *low-side switch*, the transistor sits between the LED and ground. The LED and its series resistor are connected to the supply voltage $V_S$, and the transistor opens or closes the path to ground. The LED then gets its power from $V_S$, and the FPGA only has to drive the transistor.

![Low-side switch of one LED channel as used in the prototype. The FPGA output drives the gate of the BS170 through 100 Ω, and 10 kΩ keeps the gate at 0 V while the FPGA is not configured.](images/ch2_low_side_switch){#fig-low-side width=55%}

When the transistor is on, the series resistor sets the LED current. The resistor that gives the wanted current $I_\text{LED}$ is:

$$
R = \frac{V_S - V_F - V_\text{sw}}{I_\text{LED}}
$$ {#eq-series-resistor}

where $V_F$ is the forward voltage of the LED and $V_\text{sw}$ is the voltage across the switched-on transistor. The prototype uses an N-channel *MOSFET* as the switch [@nexperia_an90001] (@fig-low-side). The prototype uses one resistor value of 470 Ω for all four colours, chosen in the same way (@sec-hw-driver).

A MOSFET is controlled by its gate-source voltage $V_{GS}$. The gate is isolated from the channel, so it draws no steady current, and the control circuit only has to charge the small gate capacitance at each edge. The *threshold voltage* $V_{GS(th)}$ is the gate voltage at which a small drain current, commonly 1 mA, starts to flow [@nexperia_an90001]. At this voltage the MOSFET has only started to turn on. It reaches its low on-resistance $R_{DS(\text{on})}$ only when it is fully opened, which needs about 5 V for logic-level MOSFETs and about 10 V for standard-level MOSFETs. A MOSFET that is only partly on, works in its linear region and turns a large part of the power into heat [@nexperia_an90001]. In the on-state, its power loss is:

$$
P_\text{cond} = I_\text{LED}^2 \cdot R_{DS(\text{on})}
$$ {#eq-conduction-loss}

To implement my prototype, different types of N-channel MOSFETS can be used. I have choosen BS170 N-channel MOSFET which was available in the university laboratory. BS170 can switch up to 500 mA at up to 60 V, and its gate capacitance is at most 60 pF. Its threshold voltage lies between 0.8 V and 3.0 V, with a typical value of 2.0 V, and its on-resistance is specified only for a gate voltage of 10 V [@onsemi_bs170]. With a gate drive of only about 2.5 V from the evaluation board, a typical BS170 is switched on, but not fully opened. For small LED currents this is enough, but it is not guaranteed by the datasheet for every part.

Example with typical values, to show how the series resistor is sized (the values of the prototype follow in @sec-hw-driver):

1. LED: blue, $V_F = 3.2\ \text{V}$ at $I_\text{LED} = 20\ \text{mA}$ [@avago_hlmp_hx64].
2. Supply voltage $V_S = 12\ \text{V}$, assumed voltage across the switched-on MOSFET $V_\text{sw} = 0.2\ \text{V}$.
3. Series resistor: $R = (12 - 3.2 - 0.2)\ \text{V} / 0.02\ \text{A} = 8.6\ \text{V} / 0.02\ \text{A} = 430\ \Omega$.
4. Power in the resistor: $P_R = I^2 R = (0.02\ \text{A})^2 \cdot 430\ \Omega \approx 0.17\ \text{W}$, so a 0.25 W resistor is enough.

## FPGA Fundamentals {#sec-fpga-fundamentals}

### FPGA Architecture {#sec-fpga-architecture}

A **field-programmable gate array (FPGA)** is an integrated circuit that contains many small programmable logic blocks, a programmable network of wires between them, and programmable input/output (I/O) blocks around the edge of the chip. The user decides what each logic block does and how the blocks are connected by loading a configuration file, the *bitstream*. The same chip can therefore implement very different digital circuits. The basic logic block contains a *look-up table* (LUT) and a *flip-flop*. A LUT with $k$ inputs is a small memory with $2^k$ entries. By filling this memory, the LUT can produce any logic function of its $k$ inputs. The flip-flop stores one bit and takes over a new value at each clock edge, which allows counters, shift registers and other sequential circuits. Besides these blocks, modern FPGAs contain special blocks such as *block RAM* for storing data and *phase-locked loops* (PLLs) for generating clock signals [@kuon2008].

All logic blocks of an FPGA work at the same time. A circuit with four PWM channels therefore contains four comparators that run in parallel. A microcontroller also has hardware timers for its PWM signals, but it handles the received data with one program on one processor. For this thesis, the parallel work is the main reason to use an FPGA. The node has to receive data, forward data and generate PWM signals at the same moment.

### Clocking, Timing and Synchronisation {#sec-clocking}

In a *synchronous* design, all flip-flops change their state at the edge of one common clock. Between two clock edges, each signal has to pass through the logic and the wires and reach the next flip-flop before the next edge arrives. At the clock edge, the flip-flop takes over the value at its input, much like taking a photo. For the photo to be sharp, the input must not change close to this moment. It has to be stable for a short time before the edge, the *setup time*, and for a short time after it, the *hold time*. If the signal changes inside this window, the flip-flop may store a wrong value. The slowest path in the design, the *critical path*, sets the highest clock frequency $f_\text{max}$ at which the design still works. The place-and-route tool calculates this value after the implementation (@sec-toolchain).

The whole design uses one 50 MHz clock, made by the PLL from the 10 MHz oscillator of the board. This frequency is high enough for a 16-bit PWM above 600 Hz and gives exactly 50 clock cycles per UART bit. It is derived from the requirements in @sec-req-pwm-clock. A single clock was chosen because it keeps the timing analysis simple and can be carried over unchanged to an integrated circuit later. With this clock, a signal has one clock period to travel from one flip-flop to the next:

$$
T_\text{clk} = \frac{1}{f_\text{clk}} = \frac{1}{50\ \text{MHz}} = 20\ \text{ns}
$$ {#eq-clock-period}

The slowest path, the *critical path*, sets the fastest clock the design can take, $f_\text{max} = 1 / t_\text{critical}$. The design works at 50 MHz only if this path is shorter than 20 ns, or in other words, if $f_\text{max}$ is above 50 MHz. In the final design, nextpnr reports a critical path of 14.54 ns, which gives $f_\text{max} = 1 / 14.54\ \text{ns} \approx 68.8\ \text{MHz}$ and leaves about 5.5 ns of margin (@sec-hardware).

The Flexlink input is the exception, because a UART line carries no clock. Its edges are not tied to the 50 MHz clock and can fall exactly inside the setup or hold window of the first flip-flop. That flip-flop may then become *metastable*, which means its output stays between 0 and 1 for an unknown time [@ginosar2011]. To stop such a value from spreading into the logic, the input passes through two flip-flops in series before it is used. How well a synchronizer works is measured by its *mean time between failures* (MTBF), the average time until a metastable value is still unsettled when the second flip-flop samples it. Ginosar gives it as [@ginosar2011]:

$$
\text{MTBF} = \frac{e^{S/\tau}}{T_W \cdot f_C \cdot f_D}
$$ {#eq-mtbf}

$S$ is the time the first flip-flop has to settle, here one clock period of 20 ns. $\tau$ describes how fast a flip-flop leaves the metastable state, and $T_W$ is the width of the time window in which an input edge can cause metastability. Both are properties of the flip-flop. $f_C$ is the clock frequency and $f_D$ is how often the input changes. Because $S$ stands in the exponent, the MTBF grows very fast with the settling time, while $f_C$ and $f_D$ reduce it only in proportion. Two flip-flops were therefore chosen. They make failures extremely rare at the cost of only one extra clock cycle of 20 ns, which is small compared with the 11 µs of one UART word [@ginosar2011].

### Cologne Chip GateMate FPGA {#sec-gatemate}

The FPGA used in this thesis is the GateMate CCGM1A1 from Cologne Chip. It was suggested by the supervisor together with the open-source tools of the OSS CAD Suite, and this combination turned out to fit the goals of the work well. Cologne Chip supports the GateMate with an open toolchain of Yosys, nextpnr and openFPGALoader [@cologne_toolchain]. The whole flow from the Verilog code to the programmed board therefore runs without a vendor licence, and anyone can rebuild every result (@sec-toolchain). The chip is also a European device, produced by GlobalFoundries in Dresden [@eenews_gatemate]. It offers far more resources than one segment node needs, with 64 blocks of 20 Kbit block RAM, four PLLs, one SerDes and 162 single-ended GPIOs in a 324-ball BGA package [@gatemate_summary].

The logic block of the GateMate is called *Cologne Programmable Element* (CPE). The chip has 20,480 CPEs arranged in a matrix of 160 × 128 [@cologne_ds1001]. Each CPE contains a LUT tree that works as two 4-input functions, as one 8-input function or as a small adder or multiplier. Each CPE has two outputs with their own flip-flop or latch, so the chip has 2 × 20,480 = 40,960 flip-flops. For this reason nextpnr counts the logic and the flip-flops in half-CPE units with 40,960 places each (@sec-hw-results).

The choice of this chip also brought one limit that shaped the hardware. The core runs at 0.9 V, 1.0 V or 1.1 V for the low-power, economy or speed mode, but the GPIOs work only with levels from 1.2 V to 2.5 V and are not specified for 3.3 V [@cologne_ds1001]. An output of the FPGA therefore reaches at most 2.5 V. This level matters in two places. The USB-to-serial adapter must accept it as a logic high, and the driver stage of the LEDs must switch at it (@sec-low-side-switching).

The hardware tests were done on the GateMate FPGA Evaluation Board version 3.2A [@gatemate_ds1003]. The board gives access to 108 GPIOs on six 46-pin headers. A 10 MHz oscillator feeds pin IO_SB_A8, the input for clock 0, and a PLL inside the FPGA turns this clock into the 50 MHz system clock of the design (@sec-clock-reset). Eight user LEDs, D1 to D8, are connected to bank EB. An FTDI FT2232H on the board handles the programming over JTAG, so no separate programmer board was needed.

All external signals use the two Pmod connectors, because they are the easiest way to connect wires to the board. They are connected to bank NB through SN74CB3T3245 bus switches with level shifting [@ti_sn74cb3t3245], whose supply is set to 3.3 V with a jumper. The bus switches do not raise the level, so the outputs on the Pmod pins still reach only about 2.5 V.

## Digital Design Flow {#sec-design-flow}

In this thesis, the path from an idea to a programmed FPGA has several steps (@fig-design-flow), every step uses an open or a standard tool, so the flow can be repeated without licences and can later be used for other devices.

![Design flow from the model to the programmed FPGA.](images/ch2_design_flow){#fig-design-flow width=100%}

### HDL and RTL Design with Verilog {#sec-verilog}

Digital hardware is described in a *hardware description language* (HDL). This thesis uses Verilog, standardised as IEEE 1364 [@ieee1364], because it is supported both by the open-source tools and by ASIC design flows. A Verilog design consists of *modules* with inputs and outputs, which are connected to build larger designs. The design is written at the *register-transfer level* (RTL), it describes the registers (flip-flops) and the logic that computes their next values at each clock edge. Only a part of the language, the *synthesizable* part, becomes hardware. The rest is used for simulation and verification.

To keep the later step to an ASIC open, the design follows a few rules. It uses one clock for the whole design, no device-specific blocks inside the main logic, and clear borders between modules. Device-specific parts, such as the PLL and the I/O pins, stay at the top level (@sec-rtl).

### Testbenches {#sec-simulation}

A *testbench* is a Verilog module that is not turned into hardware. It creates the input signals, for example a serial data stream, and checks the outputs. The testbench of this thesis checks the results itself and prints PASS or FAIL (@sec-rtl-verification). For this reason, the open-source simulator *Icarus Verilog* [@icarus_verilog] was enough, and no waveform viewer was needed. A self-checking test can also be repeated after every change of the code.

### Open-Source Toolchain: Yosys, nextpnr, openFPGALoader {#sec-toolchain}

The implementation uses three open-source tools [@cologne_toolchain]. Yosys first reads the Verilog code and turns it into a netlist of GateMate elements with the command `synth_gatemate` [@shah2019]. nextpnr then places each element on the chip, connects the elements through the routing network, and reports $f_\text{max}$ and the resource use [@shah2019]. After the result is packed into a bitstream, openFPGALoader loads it into the FPGA or into its configuration flash memory [@openfpgaloader]. Yosys and nextpnr keep their general algorithms apart from the details of each FPGA, so the same tools serve devices from different vendors [@shah2019]. The design of this thesis is therefore not tied to the software of one vendor. The commands used are given in @sec-hardware.

### Model-Based Design with Simulink {#sec-simulink-basics}

Simulink is a graphical environment from MathWorks for modelling and simulating systems [@mathworks_simulink]. A model is built from blocks such as counters, switches, comparators and memories. In this thesis, Simulink was used before the Verilog code was written, to check the idea of the data path, from the serial input over the latch and the parsing to the PWM generation (@sec-simulink).

## Serial Communication {#sec-serial-communication}

### UART Frame and Sampling {#sec-uart}

The brightness values reach the segments over a UART line, because Flexlink is built on UART words (@sec-flexlink). A *universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter* (UART) sends data one bit after another over a single wire, without a clock line, so the sender and the receiver must use the same *baud rate* [@adi_uart2020]. The idle line is high. A frame starts with a *start bit*, which pulls the line low, carries the data bits and an optional parity bit, and ends with one or two *stop bits*, which bring the line back high. A frame can carry 5 to 8 data bits with a parity bit [@adi_uart2020]. @fig-uart-frame shows a frame with nine data bits, as used by Flexlink.

![UART frame of the 9-bit word 0x176 (EOP) at 1 MBaud, with the sampling point in the middle of each bit.](images/ch2_uart_frame){#fig-uart-frame width=100%}

One bit lasts

$$
T_\text{bit} = \frac{1}{\text{baud rate}}
$$ {#eq-bit-time}

which is $1\ \mu\text{s}$ at 1 MBaud. With one start bit, nine data bits and one stop bit, a frame has 11 bits and lasts $11\ \mu\text{s}$. Because there is no clock line, the receiver detects the falling edge of the start bit and then reads each bit in its middle, where the signal is most stable. An FPGA does this with a counter at the system clock:

$$
\text{CLKS\_PER\_BIT} = \frac{f_\text{clk}}{\text{baud rate}}
$$ {#eq-clks-per-bit}

With $50\ \text{MHz} / 1\ \text{MBaud} = 50$ cycles per bit, the receiver waits 25 cycles to reach the middle of the start bit and then 50 cycles for each further bit. Because 50 MHz is an exact multiple of 1 MBaud, one bit is a whole number of clock cycles, which keeps the receiver simple.

### 9-bit UART Words {#sec-9bit-uart}

Most UART links send 8 data bits, but 9 are possible [@adi_uart2020]. The ninth bit is often used to mark a word as an *address* or *control* word instead of a normal data byte. Microcontrollers offer this as a *multi-processor communication mode*, in which all receivers check the ninth bit [@atmega328p]. Flexlink uses the ninth bit in the same way, to mark the control words that start and end a packet (@sec-flexlink). For a receiver, this is a strong advantage, a control word can never be mixed up with a data byte, whatever value the data has. A standard PC serial port does not offer 9 data bits, but the parity bit can take the place of the ninth bit, because *mark* parity makes it always 1 and *space* parity always 0. The Python library pySerial supports both [@pyserial] and the PC test program of this thesis uses this method (@sec-hardware).

### Network Topologies {#sec-topologies}

Many nodes can be connected to one master as a bus, a star or a daisy chain. On a *bus*, all nodes share one line and see the same delay, but one short circuit can block all of them. In a *star*, every node has its own line to the master, so a failure loses only one node, but the wiring grows with every node. In a *daisy chain*, each node connects only to its neighbours. The delay grows with the position in the chain, and a broken node or wire cuts off all nodes behind it.

In a cabin, the LED segments are mounted one after another along the aisle. A daisy chain fits this layout best, because each segment needs only a short link to the next one and no long lines back to the master. The present AES system is also built as a chain (@sec-sota-mcu). The weak point of the chain is its delay, and keeping this delay small became the central design goal of this thesis.

### Latency in a Daisy Chain {#sec-daisy-latency}

In a chain, every node has to pass on the data for the nodes behind it. With *store-and-forward*, the node first receives the complete packet and only then sends it on. With *cut-through*, it starts to send as soon as it has received enough, without waiting for the end of the packet. The exact latency for this design is shown in @sec-rtl.

## The Flexlink Protocol {#sec-flexlink}

Flexlink is the serial protocol that AES uses today between the master and the LED segments [@aes_flexlink]. In this thesis, the same protocol is used between the PC and the node, so that the node can later be tested with the AES system without changes.

Flexlink uses UART words with 9 data bits at 1 MBaud. A ninth bit of 1 marks a *control word*, and a ninth bit of 0 marks a *data word*. Each packet starts with a control word that gives the command, the *start of packet* (SOP), followed by data words, and ends with the *end of packet* word EOP = 0x176. The direction from the master to the segments is called the **uplink**, and the way back is called the **downlink**. @tbl-flexlink-packets lists the packets used in this thesis. All command words, including 0x176, are defined in the Flexlink specification of AES [@aes_flexlink] and are used without changes.

| **Packet**      | **Direction** | **Words**                                                  |
|:----------------|:--------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------|
| LED data        | uplink        | 0x100, 8 data bytes per node (R, G, B, W, 16 bit each, high byte first), 0x176 |
| LED answer      | downlink      | 0x180, node ID, temperature, 0x176                         |
| Count segments  | uplink        | 0x160, start ID, 0x176                                     |
| Count answer    | downlink      | 0x1B0, node ID, 0x176                                      |

: Flexlink packets used in this thesis [@aes_flexlink] {#tbl-flexlink-packets}

In the end, the node could not be connected to the AES master within this thesis, because the level shifter provided by AES for this connection did not work as expected. All tests were therefore done with a PC as the master, which sends the same Flexlink packets (@sec-hw-pc-program). Since the node uses the command words of the specification without changes, a test with the AES master remains a direct next step (@sec-outlook).

## State of the Art {#sec-state-of-the-art}

Every segment of an RGBW lighting system must receive its brightness values over the data line, convert them into PWM signals for its LEDs, forward the rest and answer the master. This section looks at how these functions are solved today and what is still missing.

### Microcontroller in Every Segment {#sec-sota-mcu}

In the present AES system, each RGBW segment has 8 LEDs in series per colour channel, controlled by four PWM signals. These come from an STM32C011F6 microcontroller in every segment, an Arm Cortex-M0+ with up to 48 MHz, two USART interfaces and several 16-bit timers [@st_stm32c011]. One USART receives the commands from the master, the other passes them on to the next segment, and the answers of the segments travel back the same way. Each PWM signal switches an LED driver that sets the current of its channel. AES uses two types. The first is the BCR421UFD from Diodes, a constant-current regulator for up to 350 mA whose enable pin accepts PWM of up to 25 kHz [@diodes_bcr421]. The second is a transistor circuit around the BC846AQB-Q from Nexperia [@nexperia_bc846], in which a Zener diode at the base and a resistor at the emitter keep the current constant.

This solution is flexible, because the protocol is defined in software. Its limits come from the same fact. The program handles the received bytes one after the other, usually started by an interrupt. The delay of each segment can therefore depend on how the program is written and on what else the processor is doing at that moment (@sec-dec-driver-ic). This delay was not measured in this thesis.

### Addressable LEDs {#sec-sota-addressable}

Addressable LEDs such as the WS2812B take a different way. The control logic and the LEDs sit in one small package, and the packages are chained by one data line at 800 kbit/s [@ws2812b]. Each LED takes the first 24 bits of the data stream, 8 bits each for green, red and blue, and passes the rest on with a reshaped signal, and a pause of more than 50 µs ends the frame [@ws2812b]. This is the same principle as in a Flexlink chain, *keep your own data and forward the rest*, done completely in hardware, and it shows that the principle needs very little logic and wiring. However, the WS2812B offers only 8 bits per colour, no white channel, no answer to the controller and a fixed protocol.

### FPGA-Based LED Control {#sec-sota-fpga}

FPGAs are already used for LED control, for example to receive serial commands and generate PWM signals in an LED dimmer [@avotins2012]. Because an FPGA works in parallel and is clocked, it can generate many PWM channels with exact timing and forward serial data with a fixed delay. Cut-through forwarding is well known from computer networks [@kermani1979]. With Yosys and nextpnr, such designs can now also be built for commercial FPGAs without vendor tools [@shah2019].

### Comparison and Goal of This Work {#sec-research-gap}

Each of these approaches covers only part of what a cabin needs. The microcontroller uses Flexlink and answers the master, but its delay can depend on its software. The addressable LED forwards in hardware with a fixed delay, but 8 bits, no white channel and no answer to the controller are not enough for cabin lighting.

The goal of this thesis is to bring the strong points together in one node. The node uses the Flexlink protocol of AES, generates 16-bit PWM, forwards the data with cut-through and sends answers back to the master. All of this runs as one digital hardware block on a European FPGA with an open-source tool flow, and the Verilog code is written so that it can later be moved to an integrated circuit. Compared with the present microcontroller, the node keeps the same protocol and the same answers. It forwards every word after a fixed delay of about one word time and generates all four PWM channels in parallel. The same code runs on every node. The LED drivers that set the current of each channel are not part of this change and stay as they are.
